blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Visual reasoning is an important capability for vision-language models (VLMs) to understand visual evidence, spatial structure, constraints, and state changes. Existing evaluations mainly rely on real-world data or procedurally generated tasks. Real-world data preserve natural complexity, while procedural games provide controllable generation and verifiable solutions. However, it remains unclear whether abilities measured in toy games correspond to real-world visual reasoning and whether game examples can support transfer. We introduce Game2Real-Bench, a benchmark that studies these connections across four capability groups, including fine-grained perception, spatial reasoning, constraint reasoning, and sequential planning. We construct 1,000 procedurally generated game samples with executable verification and curate 400 real-world samples aligned by shared reasoning requirements rather than visual similarity. We evaluate 25 representative VLMs and observe strong game-to-real consistency, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.935. We further study one-shot game-to-real transfer on four models. Constraint reasoning improves for several models, while fine-grained perception declines with game demonstrations. We also construct Game2Real-Dataset with nearly 24K verified game samples across 18 tasks and 65 QA families. Our benchmark, dataset, and code are available at https://github.com/QingAnLiu/Game2Real-Bench.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have led to substantial
progress in multimodal understanding and
reasoning ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Diao et al., 2026a ; Diao et al., 2026c ) .
Beyond recognizing what is present in an image, visual reasoning requires
models to understand how objects are related, how constraints interact,
and how actions change a scene. These demands arise in everyday tasks,
such as interpreting an assembly step, as well as in toy games with
explicit rules and controllable states. Games are particularly appealing
because their tasks can be generated at scale and their answers verified
programmatically ( Tong et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Yet their simplified
visual environments raise a central question: Do toy games reveal
VLMs’ real-world visual reasoning capabilities, and can solved game
examples support transfer to real-world tasks?

Existing benchmarks characterize different aspects of visual reasoning.
MMMU and MME-RealWorld cover knowledge-intensive problems and real-world
scenarios ( Yue et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , while BLINK and BabyVision
reveal weaknesses in foundational visual skills despite strong high-level

training ( Tong et al., 2026 ) , and VBVR-Pro demonstrates transfer to
external reasoning benchmarks for visual generation
models ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . These findings highlight the potential of
procedural training, but leave open how game-based assessment relates
to real-world reasoning across models and capabilities. A shared
evaluation linking tasks by their reasoning requirements is needed to
examine this relationship and the usefulness of game examples.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en: 2.1 Games as Testbeds for Visual Reasoning
blocks.zh: 2.1 游戏作为视觉理由测试床

blocks.en:
Recent work has increasingly used games and procedural environments as testbeds
for multimodal reasoning, benefiting from their explicit rules, controllable
states, and verifiable outcomes. In interactive settings, benchmarks such as
BALROG, LMGame-Bench, VideoGameBench, and GameWorld use diverse games to evaluate
perception, planning, memory, and decision making in LLM and VLM agents ( Paglieri et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Ouyang et al., 2026 ) .
Beyond evaluation, games have also been used to construct reasoning tasks and
training supervision. Game-RL synthesizes verifiable multimodal reasoning
problems from game mechanics, while Play to Generalize investigates whether
reasoning abilities acquired through gameplay transfer to broader multimodal
tasks ( Tong et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026b ) . VBVR-Pro further scales procedural
visual reasoning to a broad collection of automatically generated tasks with
task-specific verification ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . Together, these studies establish
games and procedural environments as effective testbeds for multimodal reasoning.
However, their relationship to real-world reasoning is typically assessed
indirectly, either through in-game performance or aggregate results on external
benchmarks. Game2Real-Bench makes this relationship explicit by organizing
procedurally generated game tasks and real-world samples around shared
reasoning requirements, enabling analysis of cross-setting
performance correspondence and game-to-real transfer at the capability level.

blocks.en: 2.2 Benchmarks for Visual Reasoning
blocks.zh: 2.2 视觉理由基准

blocks.en:
Recent advances in encoder-based and encoder-free
VLMs ( Diao et al., 2024 ; Diao et al., 2025 ) have improved visual
perception, understanding, and multimodal reasoning.
To evaluate these capabilities, a wide range of benchmarks have been proposed. General-purpose
benchmarks such as MMMU and MME-RealWorld assess multimodal reasoning across
knowledge-intensive and complex real-world scenarios ( Yue et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , while vision-centric benchmarks such as
BLINK, MMVP, and BabyVision focus more directly on visual perception and
reasoning with reduced reliance on external knowledge ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Tong et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Other benchmarks study
more structured forms of visual reasoning, including 3D understanding,
multi-view reasoning, spatial relations, and logical constraints ( Jia et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026b ; Xie et al., 2026a ) .
Recent work has also explored synthetic and procedural tasks for controlled
visual reasoning. CLEVR uses synthetic scenes to study compositional visual
reasoning ( Johnson et al., 2017 ) , while later efforts such as Game-RL, VBVR,
and VBVR-Pro extend procedural generation to broader reasoning tasks, games,
and training settings ( Tong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . These settings enable precise
control over task structure and reliable solution generation at scale.
However, it is still not well understood whether the capabilities reflected by
procedurally generated games correspond to those required by real-world visual
reasoning. Game2Real-Bench studies this relationship by combining game and
real-world visual reasoning tasks under a shared capability framework,
allowing us to examine both cross-setting performance consistency and
game-to-real transfer.

blocks.en: 3.1 Task Design
blocks.zh: 3.1 任务设计

blocks.en:
Taxonomy. We organize Game2Real-Bench around four complementary capabilities in visual
reasoning and design 18 toy-game tasks accordingly. Fine-grained Perception requires models to identify
task-relevant visual evidence from subtle local differences, correspondences,
and partial observations. Spatial Reasoning requires models to infer and transform
spatial configurations involving relations, orientation, viewpoint, geometry,
and 3D structure. Constraint Reasoning requires models to integrate multiple
interdependent relations and constraints to derive a globally consistent
solution. Sequential Planning requires models to reason over state
transitions and select state-dependent actions toward a target goal.
Individual tasks may involve multiple capabilities, and each task is assigned
to the group that best reflects its primary reasoning demand.

blocks.en:
Task and QA Formulation. In Game2Real-Bench, a toy-game task defines a structured visual reasoning
problem with explicit rules and solution criteria, while its QA families
specify the reasoning targets and output formats. These QA families
cover fine-grained visual evidence, spatial relations and transformations,
constraint-consistent configurations, and action selection over evolving
states. Across the 18 tasks, we define 65 QA families in open-ended and
multiple-choice formats. A sample is generated from a task configuration and
contains one or more visual observations, a question, and a verified answer.
The corresponding QA family further specifies any task-specific notation,
coordinate system, and output convention, ensuring consistent evaluation
across generated samples.

blocks.en: 3.2 Procedural Generation
blocks.zh: 3.2 程序生成

blocks.en:
Design Principles. Our procedural generation follows three principles. Visual Grounding. Each question is designed so that its answer is
determined by the visual content rather than prompt wording. The text specifies
the task and rules, while the image provides the instance-specific evidence
required to solve it. Diversity. We vary problem structures, spatial layouts, and visual

states from predefined configuration ranges. Given a sampled state and QA family,

ground-truth answer. Structural parameters control factors such as topology,
object configurations, constraints, paths, and state transitions, while
presentation parameters determine how each state is visually encoded and
rendered. We also retain the structured metadata required for verification,
analysis, and de-duplication.

Programmatic Verification. Each task is paired with a deterministic solver or verifier tailored to its
solution structure. Verification may involve constraint solving, geometric
transformation, state simulation, graph search, or transition replay.
Given the sampled state, the verifier recomputes the requested result or
checks the proposed solution against executable task rules. For tasks requiring uniqueness,
alternative valid solutions are explicitly checked; when multiple solutions
are permitted, all admissible answers are retained. When optimality is
required, the answer is checked against the solver-derived optimum.
Verified samples additionally pass shared checks for record completeness,
image validity, answer-space consistency, multi-image alignment, and
required metadata.

blocks.en:
We construct the real-world evaluation set by curating samples from existing
visual reasoning benchmarks and public datasets. Candidate samples are drawn
from sources containing real images, videos, multi-view observations, and
structured annotations ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2025 ; Yeh et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Pothiraj et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Xie et al., 2026a ) . We select samples whose reasoning
requirements align with those of the toy-game tasks, including fine-grained
visual evidence, spatial structure, relational constraints, and state changes.
For benchmark tasks that already meet the target reasoning requirements, we
retain their original questions, answers, and evaluation protocols. Otherwise,
we construct new evaluation samples from the source media and annotations while
preserving the same reasoning requirements. For example, for IKEA Manuals at
Work ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , we align assembly instructions with real assembly
videos and construct multi-image questions from visually distinguishable states
before and after an assembly step. All samples in the final set undergo automated
consistency checks and manual review, and samples with ambiguous answers or
insufficient visual evidence are removed.

Toy-game tasks are more challenging and provide clearer separation
between models. Most models achieve lower performance on the toy-game set than on the
real-world set, with the difference being particularly visible among
open-weight models. The toy-game evaluation also produces wider gaps between
stronger and weaker systems. For example, the best proprietary and open-weight
models differ by 16.3 16.3 , 39.0 39.0 , and 20.4 20.4 points on fine-grained perception,
constraint reasoning, and sequential planning, respectively, while these gaps
are much smaller on the corresponding real-world tasks. This difference may
partly reflect the controlled nature of the toy-game tasks, where models must
follow explicit rules and produce solutions that satisfy precisely defined
states, constraints, and transitions. Real-world samples provide more familiar
visual content and generally yield a more compressed performance range. This
contrast highlights the different roles of the two settings. Real-world tasks
assess reasoning in natural visual contexts, while toy-game
tasks provide finer discrimination among current VLMs under more explicitly
specified reasoning requirements.

blocks.en:

reasoning, we analyze model-level consistency across the two evaluation
settings, game-to-real transfer through one-shot in-context learning, the
effect of thinking mode, and representative failure cases.

blocks.en:
Game-to-real transfer with one-shot in-context learning. We study whether solved game examples can transfer to real-world visual
reasoning through one-shot in-context learning. We evaluate four representative
models on the same 400 real-world targets used in the zero-shot setting. We
construct a pool of 168 verified samples from Game2Real-Dataset covering
14 game tasks, and randomly assign one game demonstration to each target while
balancing the four capabilities across the full set. We repeat the assignment
with three random seeds and use the same demonstration-target pairs for all
models. Each demonstration contains the game image and question followed only
by its ground-truth final answer. All other evaluation
settings remain unchanged.

The effect of game demonstrations varies clearly across both capabilities and
models, as shown in Figure 3 . Constraint reasoning improves
by 4.89 4.89 points on average, with Qwen3.5-9B increasing from 24.32 % 24.32\% to 39.94 % 39.94\% . These tasks require models to abstract visual observations into
rules, relations, and valid configurations, so a solved game example may help
establish a structured problem-solving context even when the demonstration
comes from a different task. Fine-grained perception shows the opposite
pattern, decreasing by 4.92 4.92 points on average and declining for all four
models. These tasks already achieve relatively high zero-shot performance and
depend mainly on target-specific visual evidence, for which an unrelated
demonstration provides little additional information and may introduce
irrelevant context. The model-level results are also non-uniform. Qwen3.5-9B
is the only model with an overall gain of 1.49 1.49 points, while Qwen3.8-27B
changes by only − 0.33 -0.33 points, suggesting limited sensitivity to a single
random demonstration. The 2B and 4B models decrease overall, which may reflect
greater difficulty in separating useful contextual cues from unrelated task
information. Overall accuracy decreases by 1.34 1.34 points on average, indicating
that game-to-real transfer is selective and depends on both the reasoning
requirement and the model.

blocks.en: 5 Limitations

blocks.en:
Game2Real-Bench focuses on four capability groups and connects toy-game tasks
with corresponding real-world visual reasoning settings. Several directions
remain for future work. Broader task coverage. The current benchmark includes 18 toy-game tasks and 400 real-world samples.
Although these tasks cover diverse reasoning requirements, they do not span the
full range of visual reasoning in natural environments. Future extensions can
include additional task types and richer visual settings while preserving the
game–real alignment principle. Broader transfer settings. Our transfer study focuses on one-shot in-context learning.
Game2Real-Dataset provides nearly 24K verified game samples, which can support
future studies of multi-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and
reinforcement learning for game-to-real transfer. Behavioral correspondence. The correlation between game and real-world performance reflects consistency
at the model level, but does not establish that the two settings rely on the
same internal reasoning processes. Further analysis can investigate how shared
reasoning requirements are represented and used across the two settings.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We introduce Game2Real-Bench , a benchmark that pairs controlled
toy-game tasks with real-world visual reasoning tasks to examine whether
abilities revealed in toy games are reflected in real-world performance and can
transfer across settings. Across 25 VLMs, toy-game and real-world performance is
strongly correlated, while toy-game tasks are generally more challenging and
provide clearer separation among current models. Capability-level results
further show that shared reasoning requirements can exhibit different
difficulty profiles when instantiated in the two settings. One-shot
game-to-real in-context learning also reveals selective transfer, with constraint
reasoning benefiting for several models while fine-grained perception
consistently declines. We also study the effects of thinking mode and analyze
representative failure cases. These results show that toy games provide an
informative setting for probing real-world visual reasoning and cross-setting
transfer. Together, Game2Real-Bench and Game2Real-Dataset provide a verifiable evaluation framework and a
scalable data resource for advancing the study of game-to-real transfer in
visual reasoning.

blocks.en: B.3 Real-World Curation and Game-to-Real Alignment
blocks.zh: B.3 真实世界的校正和游戏对等

blocks.en:
Game2Real-Bench connects procedural games with real-world questions
through shared reasoning requirements. Alignment guides curation and
capability-level reporting rather than requiring a one-to-one correspondence
between tasks or samples. The two settings retain different visual
evidence, rules, and answer spaces. For example, Cube Net and the IKEA
assembly questions both relate a two-dimensional specification to a
three-dimensional configuration. Their connection concerns spatial
interpretation, while cube folding and assembly-state recognition retain
distinct operations, input formats, and solution criteria.

通过共同推理要求。 校正指南
能力一级的报告,而不是要求一对一的函件
在任务或样本之间。 这两个设置保留不同的视觉
证据、规则和回答空间。 例如Cube网和宜家网
组装问题都涉及二维规格和
三维配置. 它们的连接涉及空间
解释,同时保留立方体折叠和组装状态识别
不同的操作,输入格式和解决方案标准.

blocks.en:
Each real-world sample has a primary toy-task annotation recording its
designated game–real connection. This annotation is not an exhaustive list
of the operations needed to solve the question. Likewise, capability labels
identify primary demands rather than mutually exclusive skills: Rolling Cube
is grouped under spatial reasoning but also requires sequential state
tracking. The primary annotations cover 14 game task types, whereas the
full toy-game evaluation retains all 18 tasks. The other four tasks have no
retained real-world sample with that primary annotation. Accordingly, the
full-suite correlation assesses model-level performance correspondence;
it is not an estimate of the predictive value of each individual task link.

with their task-specific roles preserved.

blocks.en: C.3 Toy-Game Answer Normalization and Scoring
blocks.zh: C.3 玩具-Game 答案正常化和分数

blocks.en:
Schema-specific normalization. Toy-game predictions are evaluated against the answer schema attached to each
sample. For the 400 single-choice questions, the answer is mapped to one of
six valid option letters and compared with the reference label. For the 600
open-ended questions, deterministic parsers recover the requested values or
actions and pass them to the corresponding task evaluator. Normalization is
restricted to representations supported by that schema, such as whitespace,
letter case, recognized symbol aliases, and equivalent field separators;
it does not infer omitted values, repair an incorrect solution, or alter
the submitted sequence of actions.

司马氏特有的常态化. 玩具游戏预测按每个游戏所附的解答方案进行评估
样本。 对于400个单选问题,答案被映射到其中之一
6个有效选项字母,并与参考标签作比较。 600块
或
操作,并传递给相应的任务评估者。 正常化是
仅限于由这个计划支持的表述,如白空间,
字母大小写、识别符号别名和等同的字段分隔符;
它不推断省略数值,修复不正确的解决方案,或更改
所提交的动作顺序。

blocks.en:
Structured answers. For field-based outputs, the parser checks the complete set of requested keys
and their associated values. Reordering independent field assignments is
permitted, while missing fields, duplicate keys, and unexpected fields are
rejected. Coordinate collections are normalized where their order is
irrelevant, whereas checkpoint order, vector entries, and action sequences
retain their prescribed meaning. For example, reversing the order of two
named count fields does not change an answer, but reversing two moves can
change the resulting state. The open-answer parser must consume the complete
submitted answer, so unsupported wrappers and surrounding explanations are
not silently ignored during schema validation to obtain a matching answer.

结构化的答案。 对于基于外地的产出,解析器检查请求的整套密钥
及其相关价值。 重新安排独立的外地任务
在缺少字段时,允许重复键和出乎意料的字段
拒绝。 坐标收集工作在其顺序上正常化
无关,而检查站命令、矢量条目和动作序列
保留其规定的含义。 例如,颠倒两个顺序
已命名的计数字段不会改变答案,但倒转两个动作可以
更改结果状态。 解析器必须消耗完整
因此,不支持的包装和周围的解释是
在获取匹配答案的策略验证过程中, 不默默忽略 。

blocks.en:
Task-grounded correctness. Attribute, count, and queried-state answers require all requested components
to match their verified targets. Tasks admitting alternative solutions are
instead checked against their executable rules. For KeyPath Quest and
Growing Trail, the evaluator replays the submitted route, verifies legal
transitions and goal completion, and checks its length against the stored
optimum. Rush Exit similarly checks vehicle movements and the minimum number
of commands, rather than the total distance traveled. Laser verifies the
submitted mirror configuration through ray simulation, including the relay
order, target entry, and optimality conditions specified by the task.

以匹配他们核实的目标。 接受替代解决方案的任务为
而不是对照其可执行规则。 用于键盘查询和

blocks.en:
Order-sensitive state updates. Pipe predictions are evaluated as ordered rotation sequences. The evaluator
applies each operation to the current state, propagates water, and updates
which pipes are locked before considering the next operation. It therefore
does not reorder a submitted plan to make an otherwise invalid sequence
succeed. Mancala evaluation checks the requested board state and event fields
against the replayed transitions, including sowing, captures, extra turns,
and terminal sweeping. These checks require both the requested board components and the event
flags to agree with the replayed state; a partially correct configuration
does not receive credit.

将每个操作应用到当前状态, 传播水并更新

blocks.en:

including optimality when requested. A valid alternative solution can
therefore receive full credit without matching the stored canonical answer
verbatim. Invalid or incomplete answers receive zero, and intermediate
agreement is not awarded partial credit. Parser and simulator diagnostics are retained separately for error analysis.

blocks.en: C.4 Real-World Evaluation Protocols
blocks.zh: C.4 真实世界评价议定书

blocks.en:
Reference-independent answer extraction. Real-world responses are first converted to the output type specified by each
sample. The extractor removes recognized reasoning blocks and output
wrappers, prioritizes explicit final-answer markers, and recovers structured
values from JSON or Python-style lists when applicable. For choice and
numeric questions, type-specific fallbacks recover a candidate letter or
number when no explicit final-answer field is available. This stage uses the
response and question-side information, without access to reference answers
or accepted alternatives. The extracted prediction is then passed to the
appropriate evaluator in Table 8 .

样本。 提取器去除已识别的推理块和输出
包装、确定明确的最后回答标记的优先次序和结构化恢复

数字,当没有明确的最终答案字段。 此阶段使用

或被接受的替代办法。 将提取的预测传递给
表8中的适当评价员

blocks.en:
Choice, short-answer, and counting tasks. Single-choice predictions are compared with the reference option label.
Short answers are compared after text normalization, and counting questions
require the predicted count to match the reference. When a sample contains
multiple accepted answers, matching any one of them is sufficient. For the
CAPTURe-real subset, this is an adaptation to exact count correctness rather
than the original sMAPE metric ( Pothiraj et al., 2025 ) . The count remains a discrete target, with no tolerance-based partial credit
